leaves.title: Understanding and practicing short social exchanges
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice understanding and taking part in short, everyday spoken exchanges — the kind of quick back-and-forth you'll hear constantly in real life, like ordering something or being introduced to someone.

These short exchanges often combine several functions at once — ordering something, introducing yourself, and clarifying a name that wasn't heard clearly. Listen for the key words (the item ordered, the name given) even when several people are speaking.

Common clarification phrases:

• Sorry, what was that?
• Did you say...?
• No, it's [name], not [name].

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to follow a short real-life exchange and jump in naturally, including asking for clarification when you don't catch something.
examples: A: A coffee, please. B: What's your name? A: Marco. B: Marco, coffee's ready!
A: Are you Elena? B: No, I'm not. I'm Farah. A: Oh sorry! B: No problem.
A: Hello! Are you Mr. Diallo? B: Yes, I am. Nice to meet you.
commonMistakes: Don't assume you heard a name correctly the first time — asking for clarification is normal and polite.
'Sorry, what was that?' is more natural than 'Repeat, please' in casual conversation.

exercises.title: Complete the exchange
exercises.instructions: Read each short exchange and complete the missing line.

questions.prompt: A: Are you Sofia? B: No, I'm ___. I'm Farah.
A: A tea, please. B: What's your ___? A: Leo.
A: Sorry, what was ___? B: I said Diallo.

exercises.title: Choose what happens next
exercises.instructions: Choose the most natural next line in each exchange.

leaves.title: Understanding classroom instructions
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the everyday phrases used in an English classroom — so you can follow what your teacher asks and respond naturally when you're unsure about something.

Common instructions a teacher gives:

• Open your books. / Close your books.
• Stand up, please. / Sit down, please.
• Look at the board, please.
• Go to page...

Common phrases a student uses:

• How do you spell it?
• Sorry, can you repeat that, please?
• I don't understand.
• I don't know.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to follow classroom instructions and speak up when you need something repeated or explained.
examples: Teacher: Open your books to page five, please.
Student: Sorry, can you repeat that, please?
Teacher: Stand up, please.
commonMistakes: 'Sorry?' alone is a polite, common way to ask someone to repeat something — you don't always need a full sentence.
'I don't know' answers a question you can't answer; 'I don't understand' means the instruction itself was unclear — they aren't interchangeable.

exercises.title: Match the instruction to its purpose
exercises.instructions: Choose what the teacher wants the student to do.

questions.prompt: 'Open your books, please.'
'Stand up, please.'
'Look at the board, please.'

exercises.instructions: Choose what a student would most naturally say in each situation.

leaves.title: Introducing yourself
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the fixed phrases English speakers use every time they meet someone new — the very first words in almost any new conversation.

Key phrases:

• Hi, I'm...
• What's your name?
• Nice to meet you.

These phrases are fixed — native speakers use them almost word-for-word every time, so learning them exactly will make you sound natural right away.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to introduce yourself confidently and respond naturally when someone introduces themselves to you.
examples: A: Hi, I'm Priya. B: Hi, I'm Marco. Nice to meet you.
A: What's your name? B: I'm Felix.
commonMistakes: Don't answer 'What's your name?' with just a name — a full response like 'I'm Felix' is more natural in this context.

exercises.instructions: Choose the most natural response to complete each exchange.

leaves.title: Saying goodbye
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to end a conversation naturally in English — just as important as knowing how to start one.

Key phrases:

• Goodbye / Bye
• See you tomorrow.
• See you on Monday.

These phrases are fixed and very common — using them naturally at the end of a conversation makes you sound comfortable and fluent, not just correct.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to end a conversation smoothly and mention when you'll see the person again.
examples: A: Bye! See you tomorrow. B: Bye!
A: See you on Friday. B: OK, see you then.
commonMistakes: 'Goodbye' and 'Bye' both work, but don't mix them with 'Hello' at the end of a conversation.

leaves.title: Spelling and the alphabet
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to ask someone to spell a word or name, and how to spell your own name out loud — something you'll need constantly for forms, bookings, and phone calls.

Key phrases:

• How do you spell that?
• Can you spell your last name, please?

Answers are given letter by letter, e.g. "W-A-L-K-E-R" — never as a whole word.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to spell your own name clearly and ask someone else to spell theirs.
examples: A: How do you spell your last name? B: It's W-A-L-K-E-R.
A: Sorry, can you spell that, please? B: Sure, it's M-A-R-C-O.
commonMistakes: Say letters one at a time when spelling, not as a whole word.
'How do you spell it?' is more natural than 'What is the spelling?' in everyday speech.

exercises.title: Choose the best response
exercises.instructions: Choose the most natural response to complete each exchange.

questions.prompt: A: How do you spell your last name? B: ___

exercises.instructions: Spell each word or name letter by letter, separated by hyphens.

leaves.title: Service requests (hotels and restaurants)
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the fixed phrases used for common service situations, like checking into a hotel or being seated at a restaurant — practical, real-world English you'll use while traveling or eating out.

Key phrases:

• I have a reservation.
• A table for two, please.
• Can I have the check, please?

Staff often reply with short, fixed phrases too, like "Sure," "Right this way," or "Just a moment."

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to check into a hotel and order a table at a restaurant with confidence.
examples: A: I have a reservation. My name's Aliyah Reed. B: Let me check... Yes, you're in room 214.
A: A table for two, please. B: Right this way.
commonMistakes: 'I have a reservation' is more natural than 'I reserved' when checking in.
'A table for two, please' doesn't need a full sentence like 'I want a table for two.'

exercises.instructions: Complete each short exchange with the correct phrase.

exercises.instructions: Choose the most natural response to complete each exchange.

leaves.title: Understanding and asking about prices
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to read and say prices in different currencies, and how to ask how much something costs — a skill you'll need in almost any store or market.

Saying prices:

• £12.75 — twelve pounds seventy-five
• €15.99 — fifteen euros ninety-nine
• $50.19 — fifty dollars and nineteen cents
• 60p / 60 cents — sixty pence / sixty cents

Asking the price:

• How much is it? (one thing)
• How much are they/these/those? (more than one thing)

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to ask the price of something and understand the answer, in pounds, euros, or dollars.
examples: How much is this mug? It's twelve dollars fifty.
How much are these key chains? They're eight euros twenty.
That's five pounds thirty-five, please.
commonMistakes: Use 'is' for one thing and 'are' for more than one: 'How much are this?' is wrong — say 'How much is this?'
Don't drop the currency word when speaking: say 'twelve dollars fifty', not just 'twelve fifty', unless the currency is already clear from context.

exercises.title: Match the price to the words
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct way to say each price.

questions.prompt: A: How much ___ this postcard? B: It's a dollar fifty.
A: How much ___ those sunglasses? B: They're twenty dollars.
A: How ___ is the mug? B: It's eight dollars.

leaves.title: Ordering food and drink
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the fixed phrases used to order food and drink at a counter or café — practical language you'll use whenever you buy lunch or a snack.

Ordering:

• Can I have a [item], please?
• And a [drink], please.

Server follow-up questions and typical answers:

• Anything else? — No, thanks. / And a coffee, please.
• Ice and lemon? — Yes, please. / No, thanks.
• How much is it? — That's [price].

When you're handed your order, the server often says 'Here you are' or 'Here you go'; you can respond 'Thanks'.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to order food and a drink, answer follow-up questions, and pay with confidence.
examples: Can I have a cheese sandwich, please? And a coffee, please.
Anything else? No, thanks. How much is it?
Here you are. Thanks!
commonMistakes: 'Can I have...?' is more natural than 'I want...' when ordering politely.
Answer 'Anything else?' with 'No, thanks' or a new item — not just 'No'.

leaves.title: Asking and telling the time
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the fixed phrases for asking and telling the time in conversation, plus how to react politely when you're late for something.

Asking and telling the time:

• What time is it? — It's a quarter to eight.
• What time's your train/meeting? — At seven forty-seven.

Talking about lateness:

• You need to hurry! You only have two minutes.
• I'm sorry I'm late. / I'm really sorry.
• Don't worry.
• You're an hour late.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to ask what time it is, tell someone the time, and apologize naturally if you're running late.
examples: Excuse me, what time is it? It's eleven o'clock.
You need to hurry! Your train leaves in two minutes.
I'm really sorry I'm late. — Don't worry.
commonMistakes: 'What time is it?' asks for the current time; 'What time's your train?' asks about a scheduled time — don't mix them up.
'Don't worry' is the natural response to an apology — 'no problem' is fine too, but don't say 'don't sorry'.
